hubs.name: hub_business_entity
hubs.description: Company-wide party (business entity) register; persons share the same business entity number and therefore the same hub (one hub per business key). Integration point for sales, HR, purchasing and marketing. Email addresses and sign-in credentials attach via the same business entity number and are declared as feeds so their satellites bind to their own source relations.

hubs.name: hub_address
hubs.description: Postal address identified by its own address number, shareable by several parties.

hubs.name: hub_address_type
hubs.description: Reference list of address types (Billing, Home, Shipping), keyed on name per decided key.

hubs.name: hub_contact_type
hubs.description: Reference list of contact types (role a person plays for an organisation), keyed on name per decided key.

hubs.name: hub_phone_number_type
hubs.description: Reference list of phone number types (home, work, mobile).

hubs.name: hub_country_region
hubs.description: Country or region identified by its ISO code.

hubs.name: hub_state_province
hubs.description: State or province reference list, keyed on name per decided key.

hubs.name: hub_department
hubs.description: Register of departments, the organisational units people work in, identified by department name.

hubs.name: hub_shift
hubs.description: Register of eight-hour working shifts, identified by shift name.

hubs.name: hub_job_candidate
hubs.description: Job candidates: people who applied for a position and whose application HR holds.

links.description: Contact relationship: organisation (business entity), the person acting as its contact (role-qualified), and the contact type.

links.name: link_business_entity_phone_number_type

links.name: link_address_state_province

links.name: link_job_candidate_business_entity

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_details
satellites.description: Business entity existence and last-changed timestamp; rowguid excluded as technical metadata.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_person_name
satellites.description: Person type and name details with full history.
satellites.split_rationale: Ordinary name/contact data, separated from compliance-sensitive consent and sensitive demographics.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_person_consent
satellites.description: Email promotion preference (marketing consent) with history built by the warehouse.
satellites.split_rationale: Compliance-sensitive classification; history tracked separately.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_person_sensitive
satellites.description: Additional contact information and demographics (XML), access restricted.
satellites.split_rationale: Sensitive data classification and XML data type; restricted separately from name reporting.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_email
satellites.description: A person's email addresses, numbered within the person, with history of superseded values.
satellites.split_rationale: Own source relation at finer grain (several per person); EmailAddress is declared as a feed of the hub.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_credential
satellites.description: Existence and last-change of a person's sign-in credential; hash and salt deliberately excluded.
satellites.split_rationale: Separate source (declared as a hub feed); credential values excluded from analytical use.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_phone_number_type_numbers
satellites.description: Telephone numbers of a person per phone number type, with history.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_address_details
satellites.description: Last-changed timestamp of the party-address relationship; history of relationships retained.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_contact_details
satellites.description: Last-changed timestamp of the contact relationship; history retained.

satellites.name: sat_address_details
satellites.description: Street, city and postal details of an address with full history.

satellites.name: sat_address_location
satellites.description: Geographic location (latitude/longitude) of an address.
satellites.split_rationale: Spatial data type and personal-data classification (geographic coordinates).

satellites.name: sat_address_type_details
satellites.description: Address type reference metadata.

satellites.name: sat_contact_type_details
satellites.description: Contact type reference metadata.

satellites.name: sat_phone_number_type_details
satellites.description: Phone number type name, with history of renames.

satellites.name: sat_country_region_details
satellites.description: Country or region name with visible rename history.

satellites.name: sat_state_province_details
satellites.description: State or province ISO code and no-genuine-code flag.

satellites.name: sat_state_province_territory
satellites.description: Sales territory assignment of a state or province, history preserved; territory descriptions come from the sales area.
satellites.split_rationale: Different rate of change and business meaning (territory reassignment) from code/flag details.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_identifiers
satellites.description: Alternate employee identifiers: national ID number and network login. These are used to join data, not to anchor identity.
satellites.split_rationale: Identifier-type attributes; the national ID is sensitive, so these are kept apart from operational job data.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_job
satellites.description: Employment details: job title, hire date, salaried/hourly classification, active status and last-updated timestamp. History is built by observing overwrites.
satellites.split_rationale: Non-sensitive employment attributes that change slowly; this satellite holds the Employee ModifiedDate.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_personal
satellites.description: Restricted personal employee data: date of birth, gender and marital status.
satellites.split_rationale: Data classification: personal data restricted to authorised HR users.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_leave
satellites.description: Point-in-time leave balance readings. Changes are captured as a series of balances.
satellites.split_rationale: Rate of change: leave balances change far more often than other employee attributes.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_hierarchy
satellites.description: The employee's position and depth in the corporate reporting hierarchy. History is built by capturing changes.
satellites.split_rationale: Hierarchy position changes independently of job details and only its current value is held in the source.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_employee_pay
satellites.description: Pay rate history per employee, keyed by effective rate change date: hourly rate and pay frequency.
satellites.split_rationale: Separate source relation at a finer grain (one row per rate change); EmployeePayHistory is declared as a feed of hub_business_entity.

satellites.name: sat_department_details
satellites.description: Department description: owning group and last change date. History is captured because the source overwrites it.

satellites.name: sat_shift_details
satellites.description: Shift definition: start and end time and last-updated timestamp. These can be adjusted over time.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_department_shift_effectivity
satellites.description: Active period of each department/shift assignment. A missing EndDate marks the current assignment.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_department_shift_details
satellites.description: Last-updated timestamp of each assignment record, one row per assignment start date.
satellites.split_rationale: Kept out of the effectivity satellite, which must carry exactly the start and end dates; multi-active on StartDate because repeated stints share the same link key.

satellites.name: sat_job_candidate_resume
satellites.description: The candidate's résumé, held as a structured document, plus a last-updated timestamp.
satellites.split_rationale: Candidate personal data has its own retention and access rules.

requirements.text: The business must be able to identify every product uniquely and unambiguously.
Each product carries a product number that is unique and is used as the natural business key for the product.
Every product must carry a product name.
The product name is descriptive and not guaranteed to be unique, so it must not be relied on to identify a product.
The business must know, for every product, whether it is manufactured in-house or purchased from outside.
Whether a product is manufactured in-house or purchased determines whether it has a manufacturing route, a bill of materials and work orders, or arrives via purchasing.
The business must know whether a product is a salable item or not.
Reporting on the product portfolio must be able to separate salable finished goods from internal-only items.
The business must track product colour where it applies.
Not all products have a colour.
The business must track product size and, separately, the unit of measure in which the size is expressed.
requirements.obj: product size and size unit of measure

requirements.text: Product size and its unit of measure must always be read together.
The business must track product weight and, separately, the unit in which the weight is expressed.
requirements.obj: product weight and weight unit of measure

requirements.text: Product weight is meaningless without its unit and must be read together with it.
The business must know how many days are required to manufacture a product.
Products are grouped into a product line, with the recognised lines being Road, Mountain, Touring and Standard.
Reporting on the range, on sales performance and on manufacturing load must be possible by product line.
requirements.obj: range, sales performance and manufacturing load by product line

requirements.text: Products carry a class of High, Medium or Low.
The business meaning of product class is not stated in the source system and must be confirmed with the product management team before it is used as an analytical dimension.
Products carry a style of Womens, Mens or Universal.
Product style is a merchandising attribute and must be available for analysis of the range.
The business must record the standard cost of a product, the cost figure used for costing and margin purposes.
The business must record the list price of a product, the price at which it is offered for sale.
The business must be able to compare list price against standard cost to understand the margin position of each product.
The business must record the safety stock level for each product, being the minimum inventory quantity intended to be held.
The business must record the reorder point for each product, being the inventory level at which a purchase order or a work order is triggered.

The business must be able to compare actual inventory on hand against the safety stock level and the reorder point to identify products at risk of stock-out and products where a replenishment action is overdue.
requirements.obj: inventory on hand against safety stock level and reorder point

requirements.text: The business must know the date from which a product became available for sale.
The business must know the date from which a product ceased to be available for sale, where that has happened.
A current product has no sell end date.
The business must know the date on which a product was discontinued, where applicable.
Discontinuation and the end of sale availability must be treated as two distinct business events, and product management should confirm the difference in meaning between them.
requirements.obj: product discontinued date and sell end date

requirements.text: The business must be able to report on the active product range as at any point in time, using the sell start and sell end dates.
requirements.obj: active product range at a point in time

requirements.text: Products are organised into a two-level classification consisting of product categories, which are subdivided into product subcategories.
A product category must be identifiable by its name (its description).
Product categories are the top level of the merchandising hierarchy, being broad groupings such as bikes, components, clothing and accessories.
A product subcategory must be identifiable by its name.
A product subcategory belongs to exactly one product category.
A product belongs to at most one product subcategory, and not every product is placed in a subcategory.
Reporting must handle unclassified products gracefully rather than dropping them.
The business must be able to roll up any product-level measure, such as inventory, cost, price, transaction volume and scrap, to subcategory and then to category level.
requirements.obj: product-level measures to subcategory and category

requirements.text: The business must be able to identify a product model by its name.
Several products can share one product model.
A product belongs to at most one product model, and not every product has one.
The business must be able to group and report products by product model.
Detailed catalogue information is held at product model level in a structured document format and must be available for catalogue and web publication purposes.
Manufacturing instructions are held at product model level in a structured document format, and manufacturing and quality teams must have access to the instructions that apply to a given model.
The level of detail that can be extracted from the structured manufacturing instruction documents must be scoped separately with the manufacturing engineering team.
The business maintains a library of product descriptions, which are free-text marketing descriptions of products held independently of any one product.
The business maintains a list of cultures (language and locale designations), each identified by a short culture code and carrying a descriptive name.
A product model is associated with a product description in a specific culture, so that the same model can have different descriptions for different markets.
The business must be able to report which models have catalogue descriptions in which cultures.
The business must be able to identify which models are missing a description in a culture the business sells into.
The combination of model, description and culture is the meaningful business fact; a description is only useful when the model it describes and its culture are known.
The business maintains a library of product photographs.
Each photograph exists in a small (thumbnail) version and a large version, and each version has its own image file and file name.
A product may have several photographs, and a photograph may be used for more than one product.
For each product, one photograph is designated the principal image, used as the lead image in the catalogue and on the web.
The business must be able to identify the principal image for a product.
The business must be able to identify products that have no photograph at all.
The business must be able to identify products that have photographs but no designated principal image.
The business maintains a set of illustrations used in manufacturing instructions, which are technical diagrams held in a structured format.
An illustration is associated with one or more product models, and a product model may have several illustrations.
The business must be able to determine which illustrations support which product models, so that manufacturing documentation can be assembled and kept complete.
The business must be able to identify each document in the controlled document library and know its title.
The document library is organised hierarchically, with documents sitting inside folders, and carries approval and revision control.
The business must know whether a library entry is a folder or an actual document.
The business must be able to reconstruct the folder structure of the document library, using the recorded depth of each entry in the hierarchy.
Each document has an owner who is an employee.
The business must be able to report on documents by owner, for example to find documents whose owner has left the company.
Employee master data is owned outside this area and must be sourced from there.
Each document carries a revision number.
The business must be able to see which revision of a document is current.
Each document is associated with an engineering change approval number.
The business must be able to trace documents to the engineering change that authorised them.
Each document has an approval status of Pending approval, Approved or Obsolete.
The business must be able to report on documents by approval status.
The business must be able to find documents pending approval.
The business must be able to find documents that are still in circulation but marked obsolete.
Each document carries a file name and a file extension indicating its type.
The business needs to know the document type for archiving and access purposes.
Each document has a short abstract or summary, distinct from the full document content, and the summary is what most business reporting needs.
The full binary document content is generally not required in analytical reporting, and its inclusion should be confirmed rather than assumed.
Documents are linked to products: a product may have several associated documents, and a document may apply to several products.
The business must be able to identify manufactured products that have no associated document, as a documentation-completeness check.
A product may be assembled from other products, and the business must be able to record which products are components of a given assembly.
Both sides of an assembly relationship are products, and a component may itself be an assembly of further components, so the structure is recursive and can be several levels deep.
The business must know, for each component in an assembly, the quantity of that component needed to make one of the assembly item.
The business must know the unit of measure in which the component quantity is expressed.
The business must know the level at which a component sits below its parent assembly in the bill of materials, to support explosion to raw components and summary reporting at a chosen level.
Each component-in-assembly relationship carries the date the component started being used in the assembly and the date it stopped being used.
The business must be able to answer what a product was made of on a given date, not only what it is made of now.
The business must be able to identify currently active bill of materials relationships, those that have started and not yet ended, as the default view for planning and costing.

The business must be able to see component substitutions over time, where one component stopped being used in an assembly on a date and another started, as a design change visible to engineering and cost teams.
The business must be able to determine, for any component, all the assemblies it is used in (where used), to assess the impact of a component shortage, price change or quality problem.
The business must be able to cost an assembly from the costs of its components and the quantities required.
The business must be able to compare the built-up cost of an assembly with its recorded standard cost.
The business maintains a standard list of units of measure, each identified by a short code and carrying a descriptive name.
The same standard list of units of measure serves the component quantity in an assembly, the unit for a product's size, and the unit for a product's weight.
All quantity and dimension reporting must present the unit alongside the figure.
Figures expressed in different units must never be aggregated without conversion.
Conversion factors between units are not held in this system, and whether they exist elsewhere in the business needs clarification.
Each manufacturing location (shop floor or work centre within the plant) is identified by a name.
Each location has a standard hourly cost rate, which is used to cost the time products spend at that location.
Each location has a stated work capacity expressed in hours.
The business must be able to compare actual hours consumed at a location against its stated capacity in order to identify bottlenecks and under-used capacity.
requirements.obj: actual hours consumed against location capacity

requirements.text: A location serves two purposes: it is where manufacturing operations are performed and where inventory is held.
Reporting must be able to address both uses of the same location, manufacturing and inventory holding.
requirements.obj: location by manufacturing and inventory use

requirements.text: The business must know the quantity of each product held at each location.
requirements.obj: inventory quantity per product per location

requirements.text: Within a location, stock is stored in a specific shelf, and within a shelf, in a specific bin.
The business must be able to report inventory down to shelf and bin level, as used by stock-picking and stock-counting operations.
requirements.obj: inventory at shelf and bin level

requirements.text: The same product may be held at several locations and a location holds many products; the business fact is the quantity of a given product at a given location, shelf and bin.
The business must be able to total inventory for a product across all locations.
The business must be able to total inventory at a location across all products.
The business must be able to value inventory by combining quantities on hand with the applicable standard cost of the product.
The operational system holds only the current inventory position, not a history of it.
To report inventory levels as at past dates, the warehouse is expected to capture the inventory position over time; this expectation is to be confirmed as a requirement with the supply chain team.
The business raises work orders to manufacture products.
Each work order must be uniquely identifiable.
Each work order must state which product is being made.
Each work order states the quantity ordered.
Each work order records the quantity actually stocked, being the good output that reached inventory.
Each work order records the quantity scrapped.
The business must be able to calculate and report a scrap rate, being scrapped quantity against ordered quantity, by product, by product line, by category and over time.
Where a quantity was scrapped, the work order records a scrap reason.
The business maintains a standard list of scrap reasons, each carrying a failure description.
The business must be able to report scrap volumes and scrap costs by scrap reason in order to prioritise quality improvement effort.
requirements.obj: scrap volumes and scrap costs by scrap reason

requirements.text: A work order completed without scrap has no scrap reason, and reporting must handle work orders that have no scrap reason.
Each work order records a start date, an end date and a due date.
The business must be able to report on manufacturing lead time, measured from start to end of a work order.
The business must be able to report on schedule adherence of work orders, measured as end date against due date.
The business must be able to identify open work orders, being those started but not ended.
The business must be able to identify work orders that are overdue against their due date.
The business must be able to report work order volume and output over time, by product and by product grouping.
Each work order is broken down into a sequence of operations.
The business must know the sequence number of each operation, since the order of performance is meaningful.
Each operation is performed at a manufacturing location.
The business must be able to report the manufacturing workload falling on each location.
Each operation carries a scheduled start date and a scheduled end date.
Each operation carries an actual start date and an actual end date.
Both scheduled and actual dates of an operation must be retained, because their comparison is the basis of operation-level schedule adherence reporting.
The business must be able to report schedule adherence at operation level by comparing scheduled and actual dates.
The business must be able to identify operations that are scheduled but not yet started, started but not yet finished, and completed, based on the presence of the actual dates.
Each operation records the actual resource hours consumed.
The business must be able to compare hours consumed at a location against that location's stated capacity.
Each operation carries a planned cost and an actual cost.
The business must be able to report cost variance at operation level, work order level, product level and location level.
The business must be able to combine actual resource hours with the location's standard hourly cost rate to understand how operation costs arise.
requirements.obj: actual resource hours with location hourly cost rate

requirements.text: The business must be able to reconcile the cost derived from hours and hourly rate against the recorded actual cost of an operation.
requirements.obj: derived operation cost against recorded actual cost

requirements.text: The business must be able to roll up all operations of a work order to give a total manufactured cost for that work order.
requirements.obj: operation costs to work order manufactured cost

requirements.text: The business must be able to compare the total manufactured cost of a work order against the standard cost of the product manufactured.
requirements.obj: work order manufactured cost against product standard cost

requirements.text: Each operation identifies the product being manufactured as well as the work order.
The product on an operation and the product on its work order are expected to agree; any disagreement is a data quality issue that must be flagged.
requirements.obj: product disagreement between operation and work order

requirements.text: The standard cost of a product changes over time.
The business maintains a history of standard cost for each product, with a start date and an end date defining the period during which each cost applied.
The business must be able to determine the standard cost that applied to a product on any given date, not just the current cost.
requirements.obj: standard cost applicable on a date

requirements.text: The current standard cost period is the one with no end date.
The business must be able to identify the currently applicable standard cost for every product.
The business must be able to report cost movements over time, showing how the standard cost of a product, product line or category has changed and by how much.
The current product record also carries a standard cost figure, which is expected to agree with the currently applicable entry in the cost history.
The business requires a reconciliation between the product record standard cost and the current cost history entry, and any disagreement must be reported as a data quality issue.
requirements.obj: product standard cost against cost history

requirements.text: Historic transactions must be valued using the cost applicable at the time of the transaction, not today's cost, wherever margin or manufacturing cost is analysed over a period.
The list price of a product changes over time.
The business maintains a history of list price for each product, with a start date and an end date defining the period during which each price applied.
The business must be able to determine the list price that applied to a product on any given date.
requirements.obj: list price applicable on a date

requirements.text: The current list price period is the one with no end date.
The business must be able to identify the currently applicable list price for every product.
The business must be able to report price movements over time, including the frequency, size and direction of price changes by product, product line and category.
The current product record also carries a list price, which is expected to agree with the currently applicable entry in the price history.
A reconciliation between the product record list price and the current price history entry is required.
requirements.obj: product list price against price history

requirements.text: The business must be able to analyse margin over time by combining the list price applicable on a date with the standard cost applicable on the same date.
Cost history and price history are maintained independently and their periods do not necessarily align, so margin analysis must handle overlapping but non-identical periods.
requirements.obj: overlapping cost and price periods in margin analysis

requirements.text: Every movement of stock is recorded as an inventory transaction.
The business must be able to identify each inventory transaction uniquely.
Each inventory transaction states the product involved.
Each inventory transaction states the quantity moved.
Each inventory transaction states the date and time it occurred.
Each inventory transaction states its type, which is work order, sales order or purchase order.
The business must be able to separate manufacturing movements, outbound sales movements and inbound purchase movements by transaction type.
Each inventory transaction refers to the originating order and to the specific line on that order, which is a work order, sales order or purchase order depending on the transaction type.
The business must be able to trace a stock movement back to the document that caused it.
The order reference on a transaction is ambiguous on its own and must always be read together with the transaction type to know which kind of order is meant.
Each inventory transaction carries an actual cost.
The business must be able to value stock movements at the cost actually applied.
The business must be able to report cost of goods manufactured, sold and purchased based on the actual cost of transactions.
requirements.obj: cost of goods manufactured, sold and purchased

requirements.text: The business must be able to reconcile the net effect of transactions for a product against the current inventory quantity held for that product, as a data quality and stock-accuracy control.
requirements.obj: net transactions against current inventory quantity

requirements.text: Transactions do not record a location, so movement history is available at product level but not at location level.
If location-level movement analysis is required, the gap must be raised with the operational system owners.
The business must be able to report transaction volume and value over time, by product, product grouping, and transaction type.
Older inventory transactions are moved out of the live operational store into an archive.
The archive holds the same information as the live store: transaction identifier, product, order reference and line, date, type, quantity and actual cost.
For long-run historical analysis, the business must be able to see live and archived transactions as one continuous history.
requirements.obj: live and archived transactions as one history

requirements.text: Reporting that covers a multi-year period must not look only at the live store, because that would silently under-report.
The rule that governs when a transaction is archived must be clarified with the operational system owners.
A transaction must exist in exactly one of the live and archive stores at any time and must never be counted twice; this is to be confirmed with the operational system owners.
Customers submit reviews of products.
The business must be able to identify each review.
The business must know which product each review relates to.
Each review records the name of the reviewer.
Each review records the e-mail address of the reviewer.
Each review records the date the review was submitted.
Each review carries a rating on a scale of one to five, with five the highest.
Each review carries free-text comments from the reviewer.
The business must be able to report average rating and review volume by product, by product model, by subcategory and by category.
The business must be able to track how ratings move over time.
The business must be able to identify products with consistently low ratings, so that quality and product management can act on them.
The business must be able to relate poorly rated products to their scrap and manufacturing cost history.
requirements.obj: poorly rated products to scrap and manufacturing cost history

requirements.text: Reviewer e-mail addresses are personal data, and any use of review data in reporting must respect data protection obligations.
How reviewer identity is handled in analytical reporting must be agreed with the data protection officer before review data is published in reports.
Reviewers are identified only by name and e-mail address, with no link to the customer master.
Whether a reviewer can or should be matched to a known customer is an open question for the customer data owners and is out of scope.
Every record in the operational system carries the date and time it was last updated.
The business needs the last-updated date and time to understand the currency of the data and to detect records that have not been maintained.
The business must be able to report the as-at date of any figure presented, so that users know what point in time a report reflects.
Analysis of past periods must use the bills of materials, standard costs and list prices that applied at the time.
Past-period analysis must not be silently restated when a cost, price or assembly structure changes.
A product may have no subcategory, no model, no photograph, no document, no review, and no bill of materials, and these optional relationships are legitimate business situations.
Reporting must treat the absence of optional relationships as legitimate business situations, not as errors.
Reporting must still be able to report on absent optional relationships as completeness gaps where that is the question being asked.
The relationships between products and documents, products and photographs, models and illustrations, and models and descriptions by culture are many-to-many.
Each many-to-many association is a business fact in its own right and must be retained as such.
The owner of a document is an employee, and inventory transactions refer to sales orders and purchase orders, which point outside the production area.
The references to employees, sales orders and purchase orders must be able to join up with the human resources, sales and purchasing areas of the warehouse when those are built.
requirements.obj: external references to HR, sales and purchasing areas

requirements.text: Until the human resources, sales and purchasing areas are built, the external references can only be reported as identifiers.

Which structured-document and binary content (catalogue descriptions, manufacturing instructions, illustration diagrams, photograph images and full document content) is needed for business reporting, and at what level of detail, must be agreed with marketing and manufacturing engineering rather than assumed.
Technical record identifiers that have no business meaning should not surface in business reporting.

business_keys.rationale: REQ-002 explicitly states the product number is unique and is the natural business key; REQ-001 requires unambiguous unique identification. Stable, business-recognised, and every product carries one.
REQ-003 says every product has a name, but REQ-004 explicitly states it is not guaranteed unique and must not be used to identify a product.

System-generated surrogate; REQ-001 needs unique identification but REQ-002 designates product number as the business key and REQ-054-3 says technical identifiers should not surface in business reporting.
REQ-035 states a product category must be identifiable by its name (description); business-recognised (REQ-036), non-null.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-054-3); weak key, name is preferred per REQ-035.
REQ-037 states a product subcategory must be identifiable by its name. Since a subcategory belongs to exactly one category (REQ-038), uniqueness may need to be confirmed.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-054-3); weak key.
REQ-042 states the business identifies a product model by its name; used for grouping and reporting (REQ-045).
System-generated surrogate; name is the business identifier per REQ-042.
REQ-002-2 states each culture is identified by a short culture code; business-recognised, stable, unique.
REQ-002-2 says culture carries a descriptive name, but it is descriptive rather than the identifier.
REQ-050 states each unit of measure is identified by a short code; shared across quantity, size and weight (REQ-051).
REQ-050 describes the name as descriptive, not the identifier.
REQ-001-2 describes a library of free-text descriptions with no business identifier stated; the only available key is a technical ID, so low confidence.
REQ-007-2 describes a photograph library with no natural identifier mentioned; only the technical ID is available, so weak key.
REQ-008-2 states each version has its own file name, but uniqueness is not stated.
REQ-014-2 describes illustrations with no natural identifier stated; the technical ID is the only available key, so weak.

REQ-017-2 requires each document in the controlled library to be identifiable, and REQ-018-2/REQ-020-2 describe a hierarchical library with entry depth; the hierarchy node is the position-based identifier of an entry.
System-generated GUID; REQ-017-2 requires identification, but this is a technical identifier with no business meaning.
REQ-017-2 requires knowing the title, but uniqueness is not stated.
REQ-001-3 states each manufacturing location is identified by a name; business-recognised and non-null.
System-generated surrogate; name is the business identifier per REQ-001-3.
REQ-017-3 requires each work order to be uniquely identifiable; the work order identifier is the identifier used by the business and by transactions that reference work orders (REQ-008-4).
REQ-033-3 and REQ-034-3 state each work order is broken into operations with a meaningful sequence number, so work order plus sequence identifies an operation; REQ-050-2 adds product.
REQ-024-3 says the standard list of scrap reasons carries a failure description; it is the only business-facing attribute, though uniqueness is not explicitly stated.
System-generated surrogate; weak business key (REQ-054-3).
REQ-002-4 requires each inventory transaction to be identified uniquely; REQ-019-4 lists the transaction identifier as carried in both live and archive stores.
REQ-008-4 and REQ-010-4 say the order reference and line must be read with the transaction type, but they trace the originating document and are not stated to identify the transaction uniquely.
REQ-010-3 states the business fact is the quantity of a given product at a given location, shelf and bin; REQ-008-3 describes the shelf and bin hierarchy within a location.

REQ-025-4 requires each review to be identifiable but names no natural identifier; reviewers are identified only by name and e-mail (REQ-038-4), so the technical ID is the only reliable key, though it is a surrogate.
REQ-038-2, REQ-039-2 and REQ-043-2 describe a recursive assembly-component relationship between two products, with a start date for each relationship period.
System-generated surrogate for the relationship; weak business key.

# ADR-0001: Data Vault model derived from requirements

**Status:** Proposed
**Date:** 2026-11-15
**Decision makers:** Vault-Agent (generated) — pending human review

## Context

This model was derived automatically by the Vault-Agent pipeline from 226 requirement(s) and 32 business key candidate(s). It records the Data Vault 2.0 structures the modeler chose and traces each back to the requirements that justify it.

## Decision

Model the following Data Vault 2.0 structures.

### Hubs (16)

- **hub_product** — business key `ProductNumber`. Product, identified by its unique product number. _(requirements: REQ-001, REQ-002, REQ-004)_
- **hub_product_category** — business key `Name`. Top-level merchandising category, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-034, REQ-035, REQ-036)_
- **hub_product_subcategory** — business key `Name`. Product subcategory, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-034, REQ-037)_
- **hub_product_model** — business key `Name`. Product model, identified by name; several products can share one. _(requirements: REQ-042, REQ-043, REQ-045)_
- **hub_culture** — business key `CultureID`. Language/locale designation, identified by its culture code. _(requirements: REQ-002-2)_
- **hub_unit_measure** — business key `UnitMeasureCode`. Standard unit of measure, identified by short code. _(requirements: REQ-050, REQ-051)_
- **hub_product_description** — business key `ProductDescriptionID`. Free-text marketing description held in the description library. _(requirements: REQ-001-2)_
- **hub_product_photo** — business key `ProductPhotoID`. Product photograph in the photo library. _(requirements: REQ-007-2)_
- **hub_illustration** — business key `IllustrationID`. Technical diagram used in manufacturing instructions. _(requirements: REQ-014-2)_
- **hub_document** — business key `DocumentNode`. Entry (folder or document) in the controlled document library, identified by its hierarchy node. _(requirements: REQ-017-2, REQ-018-2)_
- **hub_location** — business key `Name`. Manufacturing location / inventory location, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-001-3, REQ-005-3)_
- **hub_work_order** — business key `WorkOrderID`. Work order raised to manufacture a product. _(requirements: REQ-016-3, REQ-017-3)_
- **hub_work_order_operation** — business key `work_order_operation`. An operation within a work order, identified by work order and operation sequence. _(requirements: REQ-033-3, REQ-034-3)_
- **hub_scrap_reason** — business key `Name`. Standard scrap reason, identified by its failure description. _(requirements: REQ-024-3)_
- **hub_inventory_transaction** — business key `TransactionID`. Inventory transaction (stock movement), fed by both the live store and the archive so they form one continuous history. Integrated from 2 source(s): TransactionHistory.TransactionID, TransactionHistoryArchive.TransactionID; canonical staging key column `TRANSACTIONID`. _(requirements: REQ-001-4, REQ-002-4, REQ-018-4, REQ-019-4, REQ-020-4, REQ-023-4)_
- **hub_product_review** — business key `ProductReviewID`. Customer review of a product. _(requirements: REQ-024-4, REQ-025-4)_

### Links (16)

- **link_product_subcategory** — connects hub_product, hub_product_subcategory. Product placed in a subcategory (optional). _(requirements: REQ-039, REQ-040, REQ-041)_
- **link_product_subcategory_category** — connects hub_product_subcategory, hub_product_category. Subcategory belongs to exactly one category. _(requirements: REQ-034, REQ-038, REQ-041)_
- **link_product_product_model** — connects hub_product, hub_product_model. Product belongs to at most one product model. _(requirements: REQ-043, REQ-044, REQ-045)_
- **link_product_unit_measure** — connects hub_product, hub_unit_measure (size), hub_unit_measure (weight). Units of measure in which a product's size and weight are expressed. _(requirements: REQ-011, REQ-012, REQ-013, REQ-014, REQ-051)_
- **link_product_model_description_culture** — connects hub_product_model, hub_product_description, hub_culture. Product model described by a product description in a specific culture. Unit of work: ProductModelID + ProductDescriptionID + CultureID. _(requirements: REQ-003-2, REQ-004-2, REQ-005-2, REQ-006-2, REQ-048-4, REQ-049-3)_
- **link_product_product_photo** — connects hub_product, hub_product_photo. Many-to-many association of products and photographs. _(requirements: REQ-009-2, REQ-010-2, REQ-011-2, REQ-012-2, REQ-013-2, REQ-048-4)_
- **link_product_model_illustration** — connects hub_product_model, hub_illustration. Illustrations supporting product models. _(requirements: REQ-015-2, REQ-016-2, REQ-048-4)_
- **link_product_document** — connects hub_product, hub_document. Documents applying to products. _(requirements: REQ-036-2, REQ-037-2, REQ-048-4)_
- **link_document_business_entity** — connects hub_document, hub_business_entity. Document owner, an employee held in the existing HR area hub. _(requirements: REQ-021-2, REQ-022-2, REQ-023-2, REQ-050-3, REQ-051-3)_
- **link_product_assembly_component** — connects hub_product, hub_product (component), hub_unit_measure.
